title: Tracking, quality and fraud
summary: How operators judge your traffic and how to measure it the same way: qualified FTDs, postbacks, cohorts and player value. You will learn to detect bonus abuse, multi-accounting and invalid traffic in your own data and keep them out of your funnel, then run a weekly quality review.

lessons.title: FTD quality: what the operator measures
objectives: By the end you can name the quality KPIs an operator uses to judge your traffic.
By the end you can calculate your true cost per qualified FTD from platform and operator numbers.
By the end you can see your traffic through the operator's eyes and predict when a deal is at risk.

steps.h: Why FTD count is not enough
steps.p: Operators do not pay for FTDs because they like the number. They pay because they expect each player to be worth more than the payout. If your players deposit once and vanish, the operator loses money on you, and sooner or later they lower your payout, cut your cap or end the deal.

d.b: Operators buy player value, not FTD count
d.s: Your deal lasts as long as your players are worth it.

steps.say: Here's something many new buyers miss. Operators don't pay for F T Ds, first-time deposits, because they like the number. They pay because they expect each player to be worth more than the payout. If your players deposit once and vanish, the operator loses money on you. Sooner or later, they lower your payout, cut your cap, or end the deal. Operators buy player value, not F T D count. Your deal lasts as long as your players are worth it.

steps.p: Most operators judge affiliate traffic on a similar set of numbers. Ask your affiliate manager which ones they use for you, and ask for them by sub-ID. Not every operator shares all of them.
d: Qualified rate|share of FTDs that meet the deal terms
Average first deposit|size of the first deposit
Redeposit rate|share who deposit again within 30 days
Active days|how many days players actually play
NGR per player|net gaming revenue each player generates
Bonus cost share|how much of revenue goes back as bonuses
steps.say: Look at these cards. These are the quality K P Is, key performance indicators, most operators watch. Qualified rate, the share of F T Ds that meet the deal terms. Average first deposit. Redeposit rate, the share who deposit again within thirty days. Active days, how many days players actually play. N G R per player, the net gaming revenue each one generates. And bonus cost share, how much revenue goes back as bonuses. Ask your affiliate manager which ones they use for you, and ask for them by sub I D. Not every operator shares all of them.

steps.p: Example: an operator report for one sub-ID over a month. Each number tells you something different. Together they say whether this traffic is healthy or a deal at risk.
steps.more: These figures are illustrations, not benchmarks. What counts as healthy depends on the geo, the product (sports or casino) and the operator. The useful habit is comparing each sub-ID with your own account average and with what your manager says the operator expects.

And bonus cost share eighteen percent, so it's not bonus-driven. These figures are illustrations, not benchmarks. What's healthy depends on geo, product and operator. The useful habit is comparing each sub I D with your own account average.

steps.p: Meta reports cost per FTD using every FTD the pixel or postback counts. You are paid on qualified FTDs. Divide spend by qualified FTDs to get the number your kill and scale rules should use.
steps.more: Example: spend $1,200. The platform shows 40 FTDs, so it reports $30 per FTD. The operator qualifies 28. $1,200 ÷ 28 = $42.86 per qualified FTD. If the payout is $40, the campaign that looked like a $10 profit per FTD is actually losing $2.86 on each one that pays.
d: Spend
Qualified FTDs
True cost per FTD
steps.say: Here's your true cost per F T D. Meta reports cost per F T D using every F T D the pixel or postback counts. But you're paid on qualified F T Ds. So follow the equation: spend divided by qualified F T Ds. Example: you spend one thousand two hundred dollars. The platform shows forty F T Ds, so thirty dollars each. But the operator qualifies only twenty eight. Divide, and it's about forty two eighty six per qualified F T D. With a forty dollar payout, what looked like ten dollars profit each is actually a loss of about two eighty six on each one that pays.

steps.h: Lab: the most you can pay per FTD
steps.p: Use the break-even lab with the qualified rate as the conversion rate. It tells you the most you can pay per FTD as Meta reports it, after qualification and your margin.
steps.more: $40 × 70% = $28 of revenue per reported FTD. Keeping 25% margin leaves $28 × 75% = $21. So your target cost per reported FTD is $21, not the $30 you might set from the payout alone.

steps.h: The operator's view of your traffic
steps.p: Example: what the operator sees for a cohort of your players after six months. If the revenue they earn is below what they paid you, your traffic is a loss for them, even if it was profitable for you.
steps.more: The operator also pays staff, payment fees, taxes and licences, so a $17 per player margin may still be thin for them. If NGR over six months were $3,500, they would be $500 down on your traffic and would likely cut your CPA. Asking for this view, politely, is one of the best ways to know where your deal stands.
steps.say: Now see your traffic through the operator's eyes. This is an example for a cohort of one hundred qualified players after six months. They paid you forty dollars each, so four thousand dollars. The players generated five thousand seven hundred in N G R. That leaves the operator one thousand seven hundred, or seventeen dollars per player, before their own costs like staff, payment fees, taxes and licences. If N G R had been three thousand five hundred, they'd be five hundred down and would likely cut your C P A, your cost per acquisition. Asking for this view, politely, tells you where your deal stands.

steps.p: Most beginner buyers measure the wrong thing for weeks before an operator report corrects them. Each fix below takes minutes and changes which ad sets you keep.

a.title: Mistake
items: Using the platform's CPA for kill rules

steps.say: Most beginners measure the wrong thing for weeks before an operator report corrects them. Celebrating F T D count. Using the platform's C P A for kill rules. Never asking for quality data. Mixing registration-date and F T D-date reports. Judging a sub I D on five F T Ds. And the fixes: report qualified F T Ds and N G R. Use spend divided by qualified F T Ds. Ask weekly, by sub I D. One date basis, always. And wait for at least twenty F T Ds. Each fix takes minutes and changes which ad sets you keep.

steps.h: A good player plays within their means
steps.p: The best traffic for everyone is adults who bet for entertainment, with amounts they can afford, and keep playing at that level. Spiky value from a few heavy losers is fragile, harmful and often clawed back. Build your funnel for steady, moderate players.

d.s: That is quality the operator, the regulator and you can live with.

steps.say: So what does a good player look like? The best traffic for everyone is adults who bet for entertainment, with amounts they can afford, and keep playing at that level. Spiky value from a few heavy losers is fragile, harmful, and often clawed back. So build your funnel for steady, moderate, adult players. That's quality the operator, the regulator and you can all live with.

lessons.title: Postbacks and events for iGaming
objectives: By the end you can map operator events to tracker and ad platform events.
By the end you can build and test a postback URL with the network's macros.
By the end you can choose which event to optimise for, based on weekly volume.

steps.p: The ad platform learns from the events you send it. Send registrations and it finds people who register. Send FTDs and it looks for people who deposit. Send the wrong event, or send it twice, and you train the algorithm to find the wrong people with your money.

d.b: The event you send is the customer you get
d.s: Clean signal in, better players out.

steps.say: The ad platform learns from the events you send it. Send registrations, and it finds people who register. Send F T Ds, first-time deposits, and it looks for people who deposit. Send the wrong event, or send it twice, and you're paying to train the algorithm to find the wrong people. The event you send is the customer you get. Clean signal in, better players out.

steps.h: The data path from ad to platform
steps.p: This is the usual path. The click ID travels with the player to the operator. When the player deposits, the network fires a postback to your tracker, which can pass the event on to the ad platform server to server.
steps.say: Follow the map from left to right. A player clicks your Meta ad and lands on your prelander. The click I D travels with them, passed into sub one, to the operator's sign-up. When the player makes their first deposit, the network records the event and fires a postback to your tracker. Your tracker can then pass that event on to the ad platform server to server, through the conversions A P I. That's the usual path, and every link in it has to work.

steps.p: Decide this map before launch and write it down. Event names on the ad platform are examples; check which standard and custom events your platform currently supports for optimisation. Names change; check the current Ads Manager.
steps.say: Decide this map before launch and write it down. Registration at the operator becomes a reg postback, and on the platform, for example, Complete Registration. First deposit becomes F T D plus amount, and a Purchase with value. A qualified F T D can become a custom event, if supported. And redeposits are usually not sent. The platform event names are examples. Check which standard and custom events your platform currently supports for optimisation, because names change.

steps.h: Set up and test a postback
steps.p: Follow these steps once per offer. Never launch paid traffic on an offer whose postback you have not tested end to end. A broken postback means the platform learns nothing and your dashboard shows nothing.

First, open the network's postback settings and note the macros for click I D, payout and event. Second, make sure your tracking link puts the tracker's click I D into the network's sub parameter. Third, paste your tracker's postback into the network for the F T D event. Fourth, make a test conversion with the network's test tool, or ask your manager. Don't make real deposits to test. Fifth, confirm it appears in your tracker, then delete or mark the test.

steps.p: For return on ad spend, send the money you earn, not the player's deposit. The deposit is the player's money and can be far above or below your commission. It also teaches the platform to chase bigger depositors, which is the wrong goal.
steps.more: Example: 30 FTDs with an average deposit of $60, spend $900. Sending deposits as value reports $1,800 of 'revenue' and a ROAS of 2.0. Your real commission is 21 qualified × $35 = $735, a ROAS of $735 ÷ $900 = 0.82, a loss. The deposit-based number hides the loss and pushes delivery toward heavy spenders, which is also a responsible gambling risk.

Spend

steps.say: Which value should you send? For R O A S, return on ad spend, send the money you earn, not the player's deposit. Follow the equation: commission earned divided by spend is your real R O A S. Example: thirty F T Ds with a sixty dollar average deposit and nine hundred dollars spend. Sending deposits reports one thousand eight hundred, a R O A S of two. But real commission is twenty one qualified times thirty five, seven hundred thirty five dollars, a R O A S of about zero point eight two, a loss. Deposit values also push delivery toward heavy spenders, a responsible gambling risk.

steps.say: Here are event decision rules, rough guides to adapt. If an ad set can reach about ten F T Ds a week or more, optimise for F T D. Fewer than that, optimise for registration, but judge on qualified F T Ds. Tracker versus operator gap over ten percent, investigate before spending more. Never optimise on an untested event. And change the optimisation event in a new ad set, not by editing a live one. Example: a twenty dollar target C P A, cost per acquisition, at fifty dollars a day is about seventeen a week, enough to try F T D. We're not certain of each platform's learning threshold, so check the Help Center.

steps.p: Postbacks should carry IDs and amounts, not names, phone numbers or emails. Player data belongs to the operator and is covered by data protection laws such as Nigeria's NDPA, Kenya's Data Protection Act, South Africa's POPIA and Ghana's Data Protection Act.

d.text: Send no personal data in postbacks unless the operator, the platform and the law allow it, and then only as the platform specifies. We are not certain this is current; check the platform Help Center and your operator's terms before relying on it.

lessons.title: Cohorts and player value
objectives: By the end you can build a cohort table by FTD month and sub-ID.
By the end you can calculate player value on CPA and RevShare from cohort NGR.
By the end you can tell when a cohort is too small or too early to judge.

steps.p: A month's total revenue mixes old and new players, so it hides whether your new traffic is getting better or worse. A cohort groups players by when they made their first deposit and follows them over time. It is the only fair way to compare ad sets, geos and months.

d.b: Follow each group of players over time
d.s: Totals hide trends; cohorts show them.

steps.say: A month's total revenue mixes old and new players, so it hides whether your new traffic is getting better or worse. A cohort groups players by when they made their first deposit, and follows that group over time. It's the only fair way to compare ad sets, geos and months. Totals hide trends. Cohorts show them.

steps.h: Example: two ad sets, one month
steps.p: Example: two ad sets from the same month. Ad set A is cheaper per FTD. Ad set B's players are worth far more. On a CPA deal the operator notices; on RevShare you notice directly.
steps.more: At 30% RevShare, A earns you $18 × 30% = $5.40 per player in month one; B earns $45 × 30% = $13.50. A's whole cohort: 30 × $5.40 = $162 against $450 of spend. B's: 20 × $13.50 = $270 against $440. Neither has paid back in month one, which is normal on RevShare, but B is on a much better path.
steps.say: Here's an example: two ad sets from the same month. Ad set A, the offer angle, has thirty F T Ds, first-time deposits, at fifteen dollars each, and thirty day N G R, net gaming revenue, of eighteen dollars per player. Ad set B, the fixture angle, has twenty F T Ds at twenty two dollars, but forty five dollars N G R per player. A is cheaper, but B's players are worth far more. At thirty percent RevShare, A earns five forty per player in month one, and B earns thirteen fifty. Neither has paid back yet, which is normal on RevShare, but B is on a much better path.

steps.p: Example: a cohort of 100 qualified players from one month, followed for six months. NGR falls each month as players drop off. That shape is normal.
steps.more: Player value over six months = $6,000 ÷ 100 = $60 NGR per player. At 30% RevShare your share is $60 × 30% = $18 per player. If the alternative was a $40 CPA, the CPA paid more by month six. RevShare only wins if players keep playing for much longer, or the RevShare rate is higher. Module 6 builds on this.
steps.say: Here's a worked example: one hundred qualified players from one month, followed for six months. N G R starts at two thousand five hundred in month one, then falls each month as players drop off, down to four hundred in month six. That shape is normal. The cumulative total reaches six thousand dollars, so sixty dollars N G R per player. At thirty percent RevShare, your share is eighteen dollars per player. steps.p: Quality problems grow quietly. One week of bad traffic is a small loss; four weeks is a clawback, a cut payout or a lost deal. A fixed weekly review catches problems while they are cheap, and gives your manager the evidence to defend your account inside the operator.

steps.p: Starting rules to adapt. The money rules come from the foundations school; the quality gates are new in this module. A sub-ID must pass the quality gate before any scale step.

Kill: cost per qualified > lower of 1.5 × target and break-even, after 3 × target spend
Quality gate: qualified rate ≥ 60% of account average over ≥ 20 FTDs
Scale +20% every ≥ 48 hours at cost per qualified ≤ 0.8 × target with ≥ 3 qualified
Operator flag on a sub-ID: pause within 24 hours
steps.say: This is the combined rule card, starting rules to adapt. Kill when spend is two times target with zero qualified F T Ds. Scale plus twenty percent, at least forty eight hours apart, at cost per qualified of zero point eight times target or less, with three or more qualified. And an operator flag means pause within twenty four hours. A sub I D must pass the quality gate before any scale step.
